newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corporate debt issuance faces skittish tone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corporate debt issuance faces skittish tone.

text.p: A still-skittish tone and prospects for more volatile trade in the fixed-income markets means U.S. corporate debt issuers will step lightly this week, syndicate officials said on Monday.
At the same time, however, issues already in the works prior to last week's back-up in yield should provide a moderate stream of supply.

J.C. Penney Co Inc's proposed $2.0 billion multi-tranche offering will top the week's issuance, managers said. The deal, set to begin its roadshow at the St. Regis Hotel in New York at Noon EST on Monday, may price as early as Thursday.

One co-manager on the deal, which is led by Credit Suisse First Boston, said the issue may be increased by as much as $500 million. There was no price talk available but the structure is said to include five tranches.
Net proceeds will be used, in part, to refinance $1.9 billion of short-term debt incurred by the company in connection with its acquisition of Eckerd Corp.

Elsewhere, Yankee issuer Private Export Funding Corp is expected to issue $100 million in debt via a ABN AMRO-led syndicate. The bonds are guaranteed by frequent issuer Korea Export-Import Bank, one co-manager said.
The PEFCO deal will be comprised of 10-year notes priced at a spread at or near 23 basis points over Treasuries.

These deals, however, do not reflect the general pace of the week, which is expected to be sluggish ahead of March employment data to be released on Friday, and perhaps the May Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

"We're up 15 basis points from last week and that is going to make a lot of corporate treasurers think twice," one manager said. "If they can hold off they will and we've already seen some people pull deals" in the early stages."

High-yielding issuers may face an even more formidable task as spreads in that market have shown few signs of reversing. In addition, dealers said high-yield mutual fund outflows of about $750 million in the latest two weeks have chipped away at investor psyches.

"The market is not going to sit down and die but there will be a greater distinction in credits," a junk bond trader said. "On top of that issues will be a hard sell because people are now talking about 7.20 percent on the long bond.
